extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for establishing, articulating, and rebutting a prima facie case of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 during patent examination and reexamination. Covers examiner burdens, required content of rejections, evidentiary standards, avoidance of hindsight, and consideration of applicant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie framework and burden-shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination and reexamination, the concept of prima facie obviousness establishes the framework for the obviousness determination and the burdens the parties face. The examiner must first set forth a prima facie case, supported by evidence, showing why the claims would have been obvious in light of the prior art; once set out, the burden shifts to the patentee to provide evidence or argument sufficient to rebut the examiner's evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted summary from ACCO Brands Corp. v. Fellowes, Inc.; the examiner must set forth a prima facie case supported by evidence; after that the applicant may submit rebuttal evidence or argument and the examiner weighs the totality of evidence in the final determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's initial burden to establish a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner bears the initial burden of using facts and reasoning to establish a prima facie conclusion of obviousness. If the examiner does not produce a prima facie case, the applicant is under no obligation to submit evidence or arguments to show nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Rinehart, In re Lintner, In re Saunders, In re Tiffin, In re Warner. The examiner must produce factual support and reasoning (not mere conclusory statements) to establish the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of an Office action asserting a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with specific citations; (B) the differences in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reference column/page/line numbers where appropriate; explicitly identify differences and proposed modifications; explain why the artisan would have been led to make the modification and why it would have rendered the claim obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of impermissible hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach a proper determination the examiner must step backward in time into the shoes of the hypothetical 'person of ordinary skill in the art' at the relevant time (before the effective filing date). Knowledge of applicant's disclosure must be put aside in reaching this determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While applicant disclosure can be used to determine differences, it must not be used to impermissibly reconstruct the invention with hindsight. The legal conclusion must be reached on the basis of facts gleaned from the prior art, not via hindsight from the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc. and In re Kahn. The analysis supporting a 103 rejection should be made explicit and factual; state the chain of reasoning used to arrive at the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and weighing of applicant's rebuttal evidence; preponderance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant properly submits evidence (in the specification, prior to a rejection, or in reply), the examiner must consider the patentability of the claims in light of that evidence. The ultimate determination of patentability is based on the entire record, by a preponderance of evidence, with due consideration to the persuasiveness of any arguments and evidence made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Oetiker and In re Eli Lilly. Facts established by rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts on which the conclusion of obviousness was reached; the examiner's decision to make or maintain a rejection must show it was based on the totality of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and types of rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit additional evidence of nonobviousness to rebut a prima facie case, such as comparative test data showing that the claimed invention possesses properties not expected by the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of experimental/comparative data and other evidence is encouraged early (compact prosecution); evidence submitted after final rejection may be denied entry into the record. Consider timing and strategic implications of submitting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of relied references in the statement of rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reference is relied on to support a rejection, whether or not in a minor capacity, that reference should be positively included in the statement of the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Hoch. Even references used in a minor way must be identified in the rejection so issues are clear and the applicant can reply appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to evaluate the claimed invention 'as a whole' and consider differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must make a determination whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious at the relevant time to a person of ordinary skill in the art, and must identify and evaluate the 'differences' between the claimed subject matter and the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of the applicant's disclosure must be set aside in evaluating obviousness-as-a-whole, but used to determine differences and to conduct the search; consider Graham v. John Deere factors as discussed in MPEP § 2141 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible bases for a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection: modification or combination of references
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103 authorizes a rejection where meeting the claim requires modification of a single reference or combination of a reference with one or more other references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on modification/combination, the examiner must propose the modification(s) and provide an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time (see Ex parte Clapp). The rationale should show how the references suggest or make the modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie is a procedural tool applicable across arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal concept of prima facie obviousness is a procedural tool of examination which applies broadly to all arts and allocates who has the burden of going forward with production of evidence or arguments at each step of examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites multiple precedents (In re Rinehart, In re Lintner, In re Saunders, etc.); use this procedural allocation to determine when an applicant must rebut and when no response is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a clear written record and rationale for prosecution and later validity/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that issues can be identified early, the applicant can reply, and the rationale may be important in interpreting the scope of any later-issued patent because issued patents are presumed valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners ordinarily cannot be compelled to testify regarding mental processes, the written record must clearly explain the rationale for decisions during prosecution (see MPEP §§ 2141-2144.09); clarity benefits later judicial/administrative proceedings and claim interpretation.
